output.title: Focus blocks come after the workflow decision
output.body:
Before you protect a focus block, decide what is actually stealing the focus.

For an owner-operator, the useful question is not whether AI sounds clever. It is whether one recurring task keeps interrupting the day: repeated customer questions, invoice data entry, or lead follow-up. If it is the same kind of work showing up again and again, that is a workflow. If it changes every time, it is probably not the first thing to automate. The distinction matters more than the tool.

A simple check: does the task follow a pattern, repeat weekly, and have a clear input and output? If yes, it is worth measuring before you spend time trying to make room for automation. If no, keep it manual and move on. No spreadsheet heroics required; a plain week of notes is usually enough. Sometimes the boring answer is the right one.

That is the bounded decision Bareni starts with: identify one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and only then define a pilot scope if it does. That sequence is an operating practice, not a promise, and the timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.

The first move is simple: name the one task, time how often it interrupts your week, and check whether it really repeats before you protect the block.
